comments.author: @rmt3589
comments.text:
This is the difference between a conductor with an orchestra, and a musician with GarageBand. The difference between an artist weaving their own canvas, and using the Adobe Suite. And engineer using sticks and vine, and using AutoCAD. 

The amount of material that has to be hand created will rapidly drop, as will the amount of other skills. You will never run out of paint with Photoshop, you will never have to recast a pianist with GarageBand, and you will never have- okay, CAD still really hard, but you get the point. Not seeing an obvious bug till the next day, spending weeks and calling friends for that one word of syntax separating a 3 year old tutorial from current software, banging your head against a project that seems so easy but you clearly don't understand something obvious so you give up on that project, these are all personal experiences, and things of the past. 

To be able to have a local coding AI, and have it look through a whole project, only for you to say "don't change the code, but tell me why this line isn't working" and get an immediate response that is probably accurate, and if not you just repeat until you do, then learn and grow. This is why AI will be great. The duck that understands your words and all the documentation, and talks back.

comments.author: @BradleyKieser
comments.text: Nonsense. At best the models can do small snippets of code but they cannot maintain a code base. O3 is particularly bad at this. Pro mode, the worst. The problem is context window. Knowledge is the key. When you are coding you need to be able to take a lot of knowledge about the system and what it should do into account. The top problem with AI coding is that it drops off functionality or changes the code according to patterns that it has found previously and this can change every single time meaning that you have an unstable code base. features that were previously tested and should not have changed can change beneath your feet without you realising it and that means a full retest is required. Often very important subtleties are dropped off causing major bugs. Brilliance in small snippets of code and one off generation is very different to maintaining a code base.

comments.author: @RLHartness
comments.text: One thing that NO ONE is pointing out about this is if you're a business systems coder, these models can help... some but they aren't any where near as helpful as you think.  I've used several of these tools and models.  Sometimes they can solve problems or offer APIs and third-party libraries that can solve a problem and give you a sample.  But as a 20 year software engineer, these models output code that I have to spend WAY more time massaging to get to work with my large code bases. I think these things must excel at "computer science" level solutions, but for the day-to-day Front-End/Back-End coder, this stuff just doesn't cut it. It's smart for complex answers, but dissecting large code bases and understanding the end result largely eludes all of these models.  At times, I don't even like using them because it can hammer out code faster than me, but I spend more time fixing a lot of the code it makes rather than simply writing it myself.

comments.author: @undefinablereasoning
comments.text: As someone with over 20 years of development experience who has used  LLMs for coding. Those rankings are a symptom of coding exams not being representative of actual real world coding problems. Coding in real life is much less about getting a function to run in o(n) time complexity and far more about understanding a massively interconnected web of logic and "weaving" features/fixes into its web. After extensively using things like Claude code and aider with various different models. I wouldn't even rank these models in the top million let alone the top ten. In my opinion, They are junior developers when it comes to ability but they do have the knowledge base expected of a intermediate/senior. I have to consistently baby sit their generation. Are they helpful for accelerated development? Absolutely, but any company that is firing their senior devs thinking they can be replaced with AI right now is likely to have seller's remorse.
